subject: Computing
source: National Curriculum KS1 Computing (uses of IT, safe use of technology, programs as sequences); unplugged activities adapted from the school's Drive Computer Science / Computing Scheme Ideas approach

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Technology around us and staying safe
lessons.title: Technology around us: input and output
objectives: Spot different technology used at home, in shops and at school
Explain that computers take in information (input) and give out information (output)
Sort devices into input and output

keywords.def: machines and tools that help us do jobs
information that goes into a computer
information that a computer gives back to us

starter: Bismillah. Name one machine you used today.
Is a torch a computer? Why do you think so?

teach.heading: Technology everywhere
bullets: Homes: phones, tablets, microwaves, TVs.
Shops: tills and card machines.
Roads: traffic lights and speed cameras.
teach.note: Show pictures of each place and ask pupils to point to the technology. Many pupils think only laptops and tablets are computers. Explain that many machines have a tiny computer inside, such as a microwave or a washing machine.

teach.heading: Input: telling the computer
bullets: A keyboard is an input.
A mouse or touch screen is an input.
A microphone is an input.
teach.note: Demonstrate typing a letter, tapping the screen, and speaking into a microphone. Say: input means we put something in. Ask pupils to act out each input device with their hands.

teach.heading: Output: the computer answers
bullets: A screen shows pictures.
Speakers play sounds.
A printer makes paper copies.
teach.note: Show a short video clip with sound, then pause it. Ask what came out of the computer to the viewer. Output means the computer sends something out to us.

teach.heading: Input then output
bullets: Press a key on the keyboard.
The letter appears on the screen.
Input first, then output.
teach.note: Use the example of a calculator: press 2 + 3 (input), see 5 (output). Misconception: touch screens are both input and output; accept this as a good observation and say we can put it in both groups.

practice: Is it input or output? microphone, speaker, mouse, screen. Show thumbs up for input, thumbs down for output.
Name the input and the output when you press the button on a lift.
Find 3 things in your room that have a computer inside.
independent: Sort 8 pictures into input and output: keyboard, screen, mouse, printer, speaker, microphone, touch pad, headphones.
Draw a device you use at home and label one input and one output.
Write one sentence: 'I use a ___ to ___.'
exit: Is a keyboard an input or an output?
Is a speaker an input or an output? Say why.
lessons.homework: Walk around your home and draw 3 machines that have a computer inside. Label whether each has an input or an output.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use real photos with labels and sort physical cards. Stretch: ask pupils to explain a device that does both, such as a touch screen.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Technology around us and staying safe
lessons.title: Staying safe online
objectives: Know what personal information is and keep it private
Tell a trusted adult if something online makes you worried or upset
Be kind and polite when using technology

keywords.def: only for you and your family to know
a grown-up who helps you stay safe

starter: Bismillah. Name one input and one output device.
Where do you use the internet: at home, school or both?
Who can you tell if you feel worried?

teach.heading: Private information
bullets: Your full name and address are private.
Your school and phone number are private.
Never share passwords except with a parent.
teach.note: Keep a calm, positive tone; do not frighten pupils. Say: we keep this information private online just like we close the door at home. Ask pupils which pieces of information they know are private.

teach.heading: Stop and tell
bullets: If you see something scary, stop.
Close the screen or turn it off.
Tell a trusted adult straight away.
teach.note: Practise the three actions with gestures: hand up to stop, close the lid, point to a trusted adult. Stress that they will never be in trouble for telling. A trusted adult could be a parent, a teacher, or a grandparent.

teach.heading: Kind words
bullets: Use kind words online.
Do not tease or be unkind.
Treat others as you want to be treated.
teach.note: Link to adab: the Prophet (peace be upon him) taught us to love for our brother what we love for ourselves (Bukhari and Muslim). Explain it as be the kind of friend you want others to be. Ask for examples of kind messages.

teach.heading: Safe or not safe?
bullets: Telling a game friend your address: not safe.
Asking a parent before you click: safe.
Telling a grown-up about a strange message: safe.
teach.note: Run a quick thumbs-up thumbs-down quiz with each scenario. Ask pupils to explain why. Reinforce the language: private, stop, tell.

practice: Is this private? Your birthday, your favourite colour, your home address, your school name.
Pretend you see a pop-up that says 'You won a prize! Click here!'. What do you do? Say the three steps.
Say one kind message you could send to a friend.
independent: Draw a poster with a character and three safety rules: keep it private, stop and tell, be kind.
Match 4 situations to the right action: share, tell an adult, close the screen, be kind.
Write or say the name of one trusted adult you could tell.
exit: Name two things you should keep private online.
What do you do if something online worries you?
lessons.homework: Teach a family member the three safety rules from your poster: keep it private, stop and tell, be kind.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use a visual three-step card (stop, close, tell) and role-play. Stretch: ask pupils to think of a good password rule, such as not using your name.

lessons.title: Sequences and repeating with loops
objectives: Write a sequence of instructions in order
Spot repeated instructions in an algorithm
Use 'repeat' to make an algorithm shorter

keywords.def: instructions one after another in order
a way of repeating steps without writing them again

starter: Bismillah. Name one thing a computer does with input.
Say a safe-online rule from last lesson.
Clap 4 times. How could you tell me to do that without writing 'clap' 4 times?

teach.heading: A dance sequence
bullets: Clap, stamp, clap, stamp.
Clap, stamp, clap, stamp.
The same steps again and again.
teach.note: Perform the dance with the class. Ask what they noticed: it repeats. Count how many instructions you would have to write for four rounds.

teach.heading: Repeat is shorter
bullets: Repeat 4 times: clap, stamp.
Same dance, fewer words.
That is called a loop.
teach.note: Write both versions on screen: the long list and the 'repeat 4: clap, stamp' version. Ask pupils which they prefer and why. Explain that programmers like to write shorter programs when they can.

teach.heading: Loops for the robot
bullets: Forward, forward, forward, forward.
Repeat 4 times: forward.
Both reach the same square.
teach.note: Return to the robot grid from Year 1. Show a 5-square straight line. Ask pupils to replace the four identical forward instructions with 'repeat 4: forward'. Misconception: pupils think repeat 4 means 4 extra, i.e. 5 in total; use counters to check.

teach.heading: Spot the pattern
bullets: Forward, turn right, forward, turn right.
Repeat 2 times: forward, turn right.
What shape does the robot draw?
teach.note: Look for patterns: ask which instructions repeat as a group. Do a human demonstration with four steps and turns forming a square on the floor if safe, or on a drawn grid with a counter.

practice: Shorten with repeat: jump, jump, jump, jump, jump. (repeat 5: jump)
Shorten with repeat: clap, stamp, clap, stamp, clap, stamp. (repeat 3: clap, stamp)
How many times is 'forward' done in: repeat 3: forward, forward? (6 forwards)
independent: Write a dance algorithm of 6 moves, then rewrite it with 'repeat'.
Draw a robot path that goes around a square, then write the algorithm using repeat.
Challenge: write a repeat algorithm for a robot to walk 3 sides of a square.
exit: What does 'repeat' do in an algorithm?
Write a shorter version of: hop, hop, hop.
lessons.homework: Make up a 4-move dance. Write it down with 'repeat' and perform it for your family.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pair actions with picture cards and let pupils physically perform each loop. Stretch: pupils write a loop inside a loop, such as repeat 2: (repeat 3: clap), stamp.

lessons.title: Predict, test and improve a program
objectives: Predict what a short program will do
Test a program and compare it with the prediction
Improve a program so it does what you want

keywords.def: say what you think will happen
an algorithm that a computer can follow

starter: Bismillah. What does 'repeat 3: clap' make you do?
What do we call a mistake in a program?
Name two things that we do when we debug.

teach.heading: Programs follow steps
bullets: A program is a list of instructions.
The computer follows each step in order.
It does exactly what it is told.
teach.note: Recap that an algorithm can become a program when written for a computer. Show a simple block program on screen if Scratch Jr or Scratch is available: move 10 steps, say Hello. If not, use paper blocks (unplugged).

teach.heading: Predict first
bullets: Program: forward, forward, turn right, forward.
Where will the robot end up?
Say your prediction before testing.
teach.note: Give a grid and ask pupils to place a counter where they think the robot ends. Stress predicting first, then testing. Ask a few pupils to explain their reasoning aloud.

teach.heading: Test and compare
bullets: Run the program step by step.
Was your prediction right?
If not, what did you miss?
teach.note: Move the counter slowly one step at a time, saying the instruction aloud. Common mistake: starting the robot facing the wrong way. Celebrate predictions that were wrong because they helped us learn.

teach.heading: Make it better
bullets: Fix any bugs.
Use repeat to make it shorter.
Test again.
teach.note: Take a long program (forward x6) and shorten it using repeat. Ask what stayed the same and what changed. Link to being patient and careful in our work, a sign of excellence (ihsan) in what we do.

practice: Predict: start facing up. Steps: forward, forward, turn left, forward. Which square does the robot finish on?
Test your prediction with a counter on a grid.
Improve this program: forward, forward, forward, forward, turn right. (repeat 4: forward, then turn right)
independent: Look at 3 short programs on cards. Write your prediction for each, then test with a counter and tick or cross.
Write a 6-step program for a friend and ask them to predict where the robot ends.
Improve one of your programs using repeat, and test the new version.
exit: What should you do before you test a program?
Write one way to make a long program shorter.
lessons.homework: Draw a grid at home, write a short program for a toy to follow and test it. Did the toy end where you predicted?
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide completed grids with a start arrow so pupils only move counters and speak the instruction. Stretch: ask pupils to write two different programs that reach the same square and decide which is better.
